name: Albert Fish

victims.suspected: 5 to 15 (contemporary police and psychiatric estimates); he claimed about 100, unverified

victimProfile: Children aged 4 to 10 in the New York City area
captureMethod: The association emblem on the envelope of an anonymous letter he mailed to the Budd family in November 1934 was traced to a Manhattan rooming house, where Detective William F. King arrested him.
sentence: Death (first-degree murder, Westchester County, March 1935); appeal and clemency plea failed
fateDetail: Electric chair, Sing Sing Prison, Ossining, New York, January 16, 1936
summary: Executed at Sing Sing in 1936. Albert Fish was convicted in 1935 of the 1928 murder of 10-year-old Grace Budd in New York after a letter he sent her family was traced to him; he also confessed to two earlier child killings.
narrative: Albert Fish, born Hamilton Howard Fish, was a New York house painter convicted by a Westchester County jury in March 1935 of the first-degree murder of 10-year-old Grace Budd in 1928 and executed at Sing Sing Prison on January 16, 1936. Courts convicted him of one murder. According to the Wikipedia article and the EBSCO Research Starters entry, he confessed to three child killings in New York that police could trace: Francis McDonnell on Staten Island in 1924, Billy Gaffney in Brooklyn in 1927 and Grace Budd in 1928. Contemporary police and psychiatric estimates attributed roughly five to fifteen deaths to him, and he made far larger, unverified claims.

The first traced killing took place in July 1924, when 8-year-old Francis McDonnell disappeared from Port Richmond on Staten Island and was found strangled in nearby woods. Witnesses described an older grey-haired man seen in the area that day, and according to Wikipedia Fish admitted the killing in March 1935, after his conviction in the Budd case. On February 11, 1927, 4-year-old Billy Gaffney disappeared from a Brooklyn apartment building; his body was never found. A trolley motorman later identified Fish from a newspaper photograph as the man seen with a crying boy that day, and Fish described the killing in a letter to his attorney.

On May 28, 1928, Fish answered a classified advertisement placed by 18-year-old Edward Budd of Manhattan, who was seeking farm work. Calling himself Frank Howard and posing as a farmer, he visited the family twice, and on June 3, 1928, according to the Great American Trials account on Encyclopedia.com, he obtained the parents' permission to take Grace to a children's party. She never returned. In 1930 a building superintendent, Charles Edward Pope, was arrested in the case and spent 108 days in jail before being acquitted.

The case went unsolved for six years. On November 11, 1934, the Budd family received an anonymous letter describing Grace's killing. Detective William F. King of the New York Police Department noticed that the envelope carried the emblem of the New York Private Chauffeur's Benevolent Association. A member said he had left some of its stationery at a rooming house on East 52nd Street in Manhattan, and the landlady there matched the handwriting to a recently departed lodger named Albert Fish. King waited at the rooming house and arrested Fish on December 13, 1934. Fish confessed to the Budd murder and led officers to Wisteria Cottage, an empty house in Irvington in Westchester County, where remains were recovered.

Fish was tried in White Plains before Judge Frederick P. Close from March 11 to March 22, 1935, with Elbert F. Gallagher prosecuting and James Dempsey defending. He did not deny the killing; the defense argued that he was insane. Psychiatrist Fredric Wertham testified for the defense that Fish was mentally irresponsible, while the prosecution's experts said he was abnormal but legally sane. On March 22, 1935, after about four hours of deliberation, the jury found him sane and guilty of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to death. According to the EBSCO entry, an appeal and a plea to the governor both failed.

Fish was electrocuted at Sing Sing in Ossining, New York, on the evening of January 16, 1936, at the age of 65. His claims of victims in many states and of about 100 children harmed were never substantiated; Wikipedia notes it is unclear what he was counting. Police also considered him a suspect in several other unsolved child deaths in the New York area between 1926 and 1932, none of which resulted in charges.

Fish was born in Washington, D.C., on May 19, 1870. His father died in 1875, and he was placed in St. John's Orphanage, where he was frequently beaten; his family had a history of mental illness. He moved to New York City around 1890, married Anna Mary Hoffman in 1898 and had six children; she left him in 1917. By the time of his arrest he had served a prison term for embezzlement and had twice been held in mental hospitals, mainly over obscene letters sent to women.

name: Anthony Sowell
victimProfile: Black women aged 25 to 53 from Cleveland's Mount Pleasant neighborhood, many struggling with drug addiction
captureMethod: Police serving warrants on a rape complaint found bodies in his Imperial Avenue home; a passerby recognized him from news coverage two days later
sentence: Death on each of 11 aggravated murder counts (August 12, 2011); affirmed by the Ohio Supreme Court December 8, 2016
fateDetail: Franklin Medical Center, Columbus, Ohio, of a terminal illness while on death row
summary: Convicted by a Cuyahoga County jury in 2011 of 11 aggravated murders after the remains of 11 women were found at his Cleveland home in October 2009; sentenced to death, affirmed on appeal, died in state custody in February 2021.
narrative: Anthony Sowell, called the Cleveland Strangler in news coverage, was convicted by a Cuyahoga County, Ohio jury on July 22, 2011 of 11 counts of aggravated murder for the killings of 11 women whose remains were found at his home at 12205 Imperial Avenue in Cleveland in late 2009. The Ohio Supreme Court's 2016 opinion in State v. Sowell puts the killings in the two and a half years before October 2009. He was sentenced to death on August 12, 2011, the Ohio Supreme Court affirmed on December 8, 2016, and he died in state custody on February 8, 2021 without being executed.

The Ohio Supreme Court identified the victims as Crystal Dozier, Tishana Culver, Leshanda Long, Michelle Mason, Tonia Carmichael, Kim Yvette Smith, Amelda Hunter, Nancy Cobbs, Telacia Fortson, Janice Webb and Diane Turner. Wikipedia, citing Cleveland press reports, lists Dozier, 38, as the first to disappear in May 2007 and Turner, 48, as the last in September 2009. The court recorded that seven women died of ligature strangulation, that Culver's injuries were consistent with manual strangulation, and that the cause of death for Long, Smith and Turner was undetermined homicidal violence. Five survivors testified to a pattern of being lured with drugs, then assaulted and choked.

In December 2008, Gladys Wade reported that Sowell dragged her into his house and strangled her until she lost consciousness; she escaped and flagged down a cruiser. Sowell was arrested but released because the officer mislabeled the offense on the report. Newsweek reported that families of six victims later sued the City of Cleveland and shared a $1 million settlement with no admission of wrongdoing.

The case broke after Latundra Billups told police in September 2009 that Sowell had choked and raped her at his home. According to the Ohio Supreme Court, officers executed a search warrant on October 29, 2009; Sowell was not home, and two decomposed bodies were found on the third floor. Over the following days searchers found eight more bodies inside the house and in the backyard, and a skull in a bucket in the basement was identified as Long's. In all, police recovered ten bodies and one skull. Sowell was arrested on October 31, 2009 after a member of the public recognized him from news broadcasts on Mount Auburn Avenue. In recorded interrogations he did not admit the killings and said he had no memory of them.

Sowell was indicted on 11 counts of aggravated murder with death-penalty specifications plus dozens of counts of rape, kidnapping, tampering with evidence and abuse of a corpse. He first pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, then not guilty. Trial began June 6, 2011 before Judge Dick Ambrose. The jury convicted him of all 11 murders and nearly every other count, acquitting him only of an aggravated robbery charge involving Wade; the court had earlier dismissed three counts relating to Long. The jury recommended death on August 10, and the judge imposed 11 death sentences on August 12, 2011.

The Ohio Supreme Court affirmed 5-2 in an opinion by Justice Terrence O'Donnell. It agreed the trial judge had closed a suppression hearing without the required findings, an issue on which the ACLU of Ohio filed an amicus brief, but held the error did not require a new hearing or trial. Justice William O'Neill dissented, joined in part by Chief Justice Maureen O'Connor. Wikipedia reports the U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari in October 2017; News 5 Cleveland reported that in May 2020 the Eighth District Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal of his post-conviction petition.

Sowell was moved to the Franklin Medical Center in Columbus on January 21, 2021 for end-of-life care and died there on February 8, 2021, aged 61; the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction said the illness was not COVID-related. He was born August 19, 1959 in East Cleveland and served in the U.S. Marine Corps from 1978 to 1985. According to the Ohio Supreme Court, he was convicted of attempted rape in 1990, served 15 years and was released in 2005.

name: Bobby Joe Long
victimProfile: Women aged 18 to 28 in the Tampa Bay area, several of them dancers or sex workers from the North Nebraska Avenue nightclub strip
captureMethod: Abduction survivor Lisa McVey gave police details of his home and car after he released her, and carpet fibers from his vehicle matched fibers found on the victims.
sentence: Death for the murder of Michelle Simms (1986; reimposed 1989) plus life sentences on eight other first-degree murder and related counts under a 1985 Hillsborough County plea; 99 years and a further life term for 1984 rapes in Pasco and Pinellas counties
fateDetail: Lethal injection, Florida State Prison, Raiford; pronounced dead at 6:55 p.m. on May 23, 2019
summary: Executed in 2019. Bobby Joe Long pleaded guilty to eight 1984 murders of women in the Tampa Bay area and was sentenced to death for one; a survivor's account of her abduction led police to him.
narrative: Bobby Joe Long, recorded by Florida prison officials as Robert J. Long, was convicted of eight first-degree murders of women in the Tampa Bay area of Florida between May and November 1984. He pleaded guilty in Hillsborough County in September 1985 and was sentenced to death for one killing, that of 22-year-old Michelle Denise Simms. According to the Florida Supreme Court's 2013 opinion, he confessed to eight Hillsborough County murders and one in Pasco County; Bay News 9 reported that authorities attributed at least ten killings to him, including that of Artiss Ann Wick in March 1984. Florida executed him by lethal injection on May 23, 2019.

The Department of Corrections record lists offense dates for the eight murders: May 10, May 27, June 7, September 6, September 30, October 4, October 14 and November 10, 1984. A UPI report from November 1984 said the first identified victim, Ngeun Thi Long, was a dancer at a Nebraska Avenue lounge whose body was found on May 13, and that the victims appeared to have been chosen from the strip's dancers and women with prostitution arrests. WTVT (Fox 13) reported that most were strangled, some had their throats cut and others were bludgeoned. The same record shows separate 1984 convictions for rapes in Pasco and Pinellas counties; Fox 13 reported that survivor Linda Nuttall was attacked after Long answered a classified advertisement she had placed; the press called him the 'Classified Ad Rapist'.

The investigation turned on a survivor. On November 3, 1984, Long abducted 17-year-old Lisa McVey as she rode her bicycle home from work, held her about 26 hours and sexually assaulted her before releasing her. She left fingerprints in his apartment and gave detectives details about the apartment, the car and an ATM withdrawal she had overheard. Long was arrested on November 16, 1984, and charged with her kidnapping and sexual battery. UPI reported that carpet-fiber analysis linked him to the murders and that after his arrest he told police where to find one victim's body.

According to the Florida Supreme Court, Long waived his Miranda rights in the McVey case and, when questioning turned to the unsolved homicides, confessed to nine murders even though no attorney was provided after he suggested he might need one. A Pasco County jury first convicted him of murdering 18-year-old Virginia Johnson, and he was sentenced to death on May 3, 1985. On September 23, 1985, he pleaded guilty in Hillsborough County to eight counts of first-degree murder, nine of kidnapping, eight of sexual battery and a probation violation, according to the Eleventh Circuit; the state agreed not to seek death except for Simms. A jury recommended death for Simms by an 11-1 vote, and the sentence was imposed on July 25, 1986.

The Florida Supreme Court vacated that death sentence on June 30, 1988. A second jury unanimously recommended death, the sentence was reimposed on July 21, 1989, and the court affirmed it on October 15, 1992. The Pasco County case went differently: the Florida Supreme Court vacated the Johnson conviction in 1987 and 1992, holding the confession had been obtained in violation of his right to counsel, and on March 6, 1997 reversed it a third time and directed an acquittal.

Courts rejected later postconviction claims, including Florida Supreme Court rulings in 2013, 2016 and 2018 and a federal habeas petition. Governor Ron DeSantis signed his death warrant on April 23, 2019. Final motions argued that the sedative etomidate in Florida's lethal injection protocol was dangerous given his epilepsy and brain injury; the Florida Supreme Court denied relief on May 17, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of a stay on May 22, finding the claims barred by delay and res judicata. Long was pronounced dead at 6:55 p.m. on May 23, 2019, at Florida State Prison. Lisa McVey, by then a Hillsborough County sheriff's deputy named Lisa Noland, witnessed the execution.

Long was born on October 14, 1953, in Kenova, West Virginia. According to the Wikipedia article, he suffered childhood head injuries, married in 1974, divorced in 1980 and moved to the Tampa Bay area in 1983. The 1984 UPI report described him as a 31-year-old out-of-work radiology technician.

name: Carl Panzram

victims.suspected: 5 corroborated by investigators; Panzram also claimed killings in Portuguese Angola

victimProfile: Boys and young men, including sailors, hitchhikers and a 14-year-old newsboy; the one proven victim was a 47-year-old prison laundry foreman
captureMethod: Arrested in Baltimore on a Washington, D.C., burglary charge; he volunteered his murder confessions while held in the District jail and later in a written autobiography.
sentence: Death by hanging (1930) for the 1929 murder of Robert Warnke; earlier 25-year federal sentence (1928) for burglary in Washington, D.C.
fateDetail: Hanged at the United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth, Kansas, on September 5, 1930
summary: Executed 1930. Carl Panzram, a career burglar, confessed in 1928 to 21 murders in several states and abroad; he was convicted of only one, the 1929 killing of a Leavenworth prison foreman, and was hanged in Kansas.
narrative: Carl Panzram was a career burglar and prison escapee who, after his arrest in 1928, confessed in writing to 21 murders committed between about 1920 and 1928 in New York, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Pennsylvania and Portuguese Angola. He was convicted of one murder: the June 20, 1929 killing of Robert G. Warnke, a civilian laundry foreman at the United States Penitentiary at Leavenworth, Kansas. According to the Federal Bureau of Prisons, he was convicted of that murder, sentenced to hang and executed at Leavenworth on September 5, 1930. The San Diego State University finding aid for his papers notes that his prison records show convictions only for burglary and larceny apart from the Leavenworth murder.

Panzram's own account, as summarized in the Wikipedia article drawn from his autobiography, begins in 1920, when he said he lured sailors from New York port bars aboard a stolen yacht and shot them, dumping the bodies in Long Island Sound. He said that in 1921 and 1922, in Portuguese Angola, he killed a boy and six men. In July 1922 he said he beat a boy to death in Salem, Massachusetts; the article identifies the victim as Henry McMahon. He also described strangling a boy near New Haven, Connecticut, in 1922 and shooting a man near Kingston, New York, in 1923. Investigators corroborated only five of the confessed killings.

The last confessed murder was that of Alexander Uszacke, a 14-year-old newsboy, in Philadelphia in the summer of 1928. On August 30, 1928, Panzram was arrested in Baltimore on a Washington, D.C., burglary charge. Held at the Washington Asylum and Jail, he volunteered confessions to the boys' killings. Philadelphia authorities indicted him for the Uszacke murder, but he was never tried on it. In Washington he was convicted of burglary and, according to the finding aid, sentenced to 25 years, to be served at Leavenworth; Wikipedia gives the sentence as 25 years to life.

In the District jail a young guard, Henry Lesser, befriended him. The finding aid records that Lesser encouraged Panzram to write his life story and smuggled the pages out. In that manuscript Panzram stated that he had murdered 21 people, committed more than a thousand sexual assaults on males and thousands of burglaries and arsons, and felt no remorse. The finding aid notes that elsewhere he boasted of 23 killings.

Within a year of his transfer to Leavenworth, Panzram killed again. The Bureau of Prisons reports that on the morning of June 20, 1929, Warnke, a 47-year-old Army veteran from Cleveland, Ohio, employed at the prison since 1921, was struck on the head with a heavy flat iron shortly after reporting to the laundry. The first responding officer subdued Panzram, who was placed in isolation and refused to make a statement. The Bureau says there was no known conflict between the two men.

Panzram was tried in federal court in 1930 for Warnke's murder, convicted and sentenced to death. The finding aid states that the psychiatrist Karl Menninger examined him and found him of sound mind at the time of the killing. Panzram refused to let anyone appeal on his behalf and, according to Wikipedia, rejected efforts by opponents of capital punishment to seek clemency for him. He was hanged at Leavenworth on September 5, 1930.

Lesser kept the manuscript for four decades. Parts of it appeared in 1970 in Killer: A Journal of Murder by Thomas E. Gaddis and James O. Long, later adapted into a 1995 film. In 1980 Lesser donated the papers to San Diego State University.

Panzram was born Charles Panzram on a farm near East Grand Forks, Minnesota, to immigrants from East Prussia; Wikipedia gives his birth date as June 28, 1891, the finding aid June 28, 1892. According to the Grand Forks Herald, his father left when he was eight and he was first arrested at eleven for burglary. He was sent to the state training school at Red Wing, where he said staff beat and sexually assaulted him, claims not independently verified. From his teens he passed through the Fort Leavenworth military barracks, the Montana State Prison, the Oregon State Penitentiary, Sing Sing and Clinton Prison, escaping several times.

name: Charles Cullen

victims.suspected: Up to 40 by Cullen's own estimate

victimProfile: Hospital and nursing-home patients, mostly elderly but as young as 21, under his care as a nurse
captureMethod: Somerset Medical Center reported unexplained digoxin overdoses; detectives traced his drug-dispensing records and a nurse colleague wore a wire, after which he confessed
sentence: 11 consecutive life terms in New Jersey (March 2, 2006); six life terms in Lehigh County and life without parole in Northampton County, Pennsylvania (March 10, 2006); 18 life terms in all
fateDetail: New Jersey State Prison, Trenton
summary: Imprisoned. Former nurse who pleaded guilty to murdering 29 patients with drug overdoses at New Jersey and Pennsylvania hospitals from 1988 to 2003; sentenced in 2006 to 18 life terms. He has estimated his own toll at up to 40.
narrative: Charles Cullen is a former nurse who pleaded guilty to murdering 29 patients at hospitals and a nursing home in New Jersey and Pennsylvania between 1988 and 2003. The Associated Press reported that he pleaded guilty to 22 murders and three attempted murders in New Jersey and seven murders and three attempted murders in Pennsylvania, and that prosecutors in seven counties agreed not to seek the death penalty in return for his help identifying victims. In March 2006 he received 11 consecutive life terms in New Jersey and seven more in Pennsylvania, 18 in all, and is held at New Jersey State Prison in Trenton. Cullen has said he may have killed up to 40 patients; that is his own estimate, not a court finding.

According to the AP, the earliest known killing was that of John W. Yengo, a 72-year-old Jersey City municipal judge treated at Saint Barnabas Medical Center in Livingston, New Jersey, in 1988; Cullen admitted putting lidocaine into his intravenous line. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that he injected lethal doses of drugs, chiefly the heart medication digoxin but also insulin and lidocaine, into patients' IV lines or fluid bags at about ten facilities over 16 years. The Superior Court of Pennsylvania, in a 2010 opinion in civil suits against St. Luke's Hospital in Bethlehem, recorded that he worked in its coronary care unit from June 2000 until June 2002, when the hospital accepted his resignation after confronting him about diverted medications, and that he later confessed to killing five named St. Luke's patients, Irene Krapf, Samuel Spangler, Paul Galgon, William Park and Daniel George.

Cullen joined Somerset Medical Center in Somerville, New Jersey, in September 2002. According to CBS News's 60 Minutes, the 2003 death of the Rev. Florian Gall with very high digoxin levels was the second unexplained overdose in two weeks, prompting a pharmacist to alert the state poison control center. The Pennsylvania opinion records that Somerset attributed abnormal lab results to Cullen and fired him in October 2003. Somerset County detectives then built a case with the help of Amy Loughren, a nurse and friend of Cullen's, who reviewed drug-dispensing records, recorded calls and wore a wire at a restaurant meeting with him, CBS reported. He was arrested in December 2003 and confessed that month to New Jersey State Police to killing patients in both states.

The pleas came in stages. In April 2004 Cullen pleaded guilty in Somerset County to 13 murders and two attempted murders at Somerset. In December 2004, the AP reported, he pleaded guilty in Newark to the Yengo murder, bringing his admitted total to 24 murders. In June 2005 he admitted five more digoxin killings, reaching 29. On March 2, 2006, Superior Court Judge Paul Armstrong in Somerville imposed 11 consecutive life terms as victims' relatives addressed him; Cullen said he had nothing to say. On March 10, 2006, Lehigh County President Judge William Platt imposed six life sentences after Cullen repeatedly demanded the judge step down and was gagged, and a Northampton County judge sentenced him in absentia to life without parole for the 1998 death of Ottomar Schramm at Easton Hospital.

In August 2006, with the sentencing judge's permission, Cullen donated a kidney to a New York man, the Inquirer reported. The case produced New Jersey's Cullen Law requiring health care employers to report misconduct, and in 2010 the Pennsylvania Superior Court held that St. Luke's had a duty to tell next of kin when it should have known an employee had killed a patient. In a 2013 interview with 60 Minutes, Cullen said he had thought he was ending suffering but did not know whether he would have stopped. The 2022 Netflix film The Good Nurse dramatized the case.

Cullen was born in West Orange, New Jersey, on February 22, 1960, the youngest of eight children. According to the Wikipedia article, he served in the United States Navy before a 1984 discharge that followed psychiatric admissions, graduated from nursing school in Montclair and started at Saint Barnabas in 1987; he had a history of depression and suicide attempts. Detectives told the AP that Cullen said he acted out of depression; prosecutors rejected his mercy-killing explanation.

summary: Executed in Florida in 2006. Danny Rolling pleaded guilty in 1994 to murdering five college students in Gainesville in August 1990 and, days before his execution, confessed in writing to the 1989 killing of three members of the Grissom family in Shreveport, Louisiana.
narrative: Danny Harold Rolling, known as the Gainesville Ripper, murdered five college students in Gainesville, Florida, over four days in August 1990 and later confessed to killing three members of a family in Shreveport, Louisiana, in November 1989. He pleaded guilty in February 1994 to five counts of first-degree murder, was sentenced to death that April, and was executed by the State of Florida on October 25, 2006. Courts convicted him of five murders. He confessed to eight. Louisiana authorities attributed the three Shreveport deaths to him but never charged him.

The earliest killings attributed to Rolling took place in his hometown. ABC News reported that William Grissom, his daughter Julie and his grandson Sean were killed in Shreveport on November 4, 1989; the Wikipedia article gives their ages as 55, 24 and 8. Investigators later noted that the posing of the bodies and tape residue at that scene resembled what was found in Gainesville a year later.

According to the Florida Commission on Capital Cases record, Rolling broke into three student apartments in Gainesville while armed with a pistol and a knife. On August 24, 1990, he killed Sonja Larson, 18, and Christina Powell, 17, in the apartment they shared. On August 25 he killed Christa Hoyt, 18, a Santa Fe College student, after watching her apartment the previous day. On August 27 he entered an apartment shared by Manuel Taboada and Tracy Paules, both 23, killed Taboada in his bedroom and then killed Paules. The victims were stabbed; the court record describes sexual battery in each incident and the posing of bodies.

The investigation first focused on Edward Humphrey, an 18-year-old student arrested days after the murders on an unrelated charge, but ABC News reported that his type A blood did not match the type B semen found at all three scenes, and he was cleared. Rolling had been booked into the Marion County Jail on September 7, 1990, for a supermarket robbery; police did not know the killer was already in custody. In November 1990, Cindy Juracich, who knew Rolling from a Shreveport church, called Crime Stoppers to name him, and investigator Don Maines found the Grissom scene strikingly similar. Rolling's blood was type B, a screwdriver from his abandoned campsite matched pry marks at the Gainesville doors, and the AP reported that DNA taken after the robbery arrest linked him to the murders. A grand jury indicted him on five counts of first-degree murder on November 15, 1991.

According to the Florida Supreme Court's 2006 opinion, Rolling initially pleaded not guilty but on February 15, 1994, the day his trial was to begin, pleaded guilty to five counts of first-degree murder, three counts of sexual battery and three counts of armed burglary with battery. On March 24, 1994, the penalty-phase jury recommended death for each murder by a 12-0 vote, and on April 20, 1994, Circuit Judge Stanley R. Morris sentenced him to death on the murder counts and to life terms on the remaining charges.

The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and death sentences on March 20, 1997, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied review that November. State postconviction relief was denied and the denial affirmed in June 2002; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of federal habeas relief in February 2006. Governor Jeb Bush signed a death warrant on September 22, 2006, and the Florida Supreme Court rejected a final lethal-injection challenge on October 18, 2006.

Rolling was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison and pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. on October 25, 2006. The AP reported that he made no final statement and instead sang a hymn. Shortly before the execution he handed his spiritual adviser a handwritten confession stating that he alone had killed Julie, Tom and Sean Grissom in Shreveport and that Julie Grissom's former fiance was innocent; the AP published the note two days later.

Rolling was born in Shreveport on May 26, 1954. According to the Wikipedia article, his father was a Shreveport police officer who abused his wife and sons. The AP reported that he served about eight years in prison in Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi for robberies before the Gainesville killings.

captureMethod: Never arrested; accomplice Elmer Wayne Henley shot him dead on August 8, 1973 and then led police to the burial sites.
fateDetail: Shot by accomplice Elmer Wayne Henley at 2020 Lamar Drive, Pasadena, Texas; the shooting was ruled self-defense
summary: Killed by his accomplice in 1973 and never charged. Dean Corll, Houston's 'Candy Man', is linked by police to 28 murders of boys and young men from 1970 to 1973; accomplices Elmer Wayne Henley and David Brooks were convicted.
narrative: Dean Arnold Corll was a Houston, Texas, electrician who, with two teenage accomplices, abducted and killed teenage boys and young men between 1970 and 1973. He was never arrested or charged. On August 8, 1973, his accomplice Elmer Wayne Henley, then 17, shot him dead at Corll's house in Pasadena, Texas, a killing authorities ruled self-defense. Houston police attributed 28 victims to Corll, and 27 bodies were recovered in August 1973. Henley and the second accomplice, David Owen Brooks, were both convicted of murder and sentenced to life terms.

According to the Wikipedia article, which draws on contemporary reporting and later investigations, the first known victim was Jeffrey Alan Konen, killed on September 25, 1970, and the last was James Stanton Dreymala, 13, killed on August 3, 1973. Victims were aged 13 to 20, and most were taken from the Houston Heights, a working-class neighborhood northwest of downtown. They were lured with the offer of a party or a ride, restrained, sexually assaulted and killed by strangulation or with a .22-caliber pistol. The bodies were buried in a rented boat shed in southwest Houston, on the beach at High Island on the Bolivar Peninsula and in woods near Lake Sam Rayburn.

The crimes came to light on the morning of August 8, 1973, when Henley telephoned Pasadena police to say he had shot Corll. ABC13 reported that Henley told officers Corll had tortured and murdered teenagers and that he and Brooks then led investigators to the graves. Police recovered 17 bodies from the boat shed on Silver Bell Street, four near Lake Sam Rayburn and six at High Island, for a total of 27. Brooks turned himself in the day after Henley's arrest. Police halted the search on August 13, 1973, after the 27th body was found, although Henley maintained that more victims were buried at the beach and in the shed.

A Harris County grand jury returned indictments on August 14, 1973: Henley on six murders and Brooks on four. Henley was tried in San Antonio in July 1974, convicted by a jury of six murders and sentenced to six consecutive 99-year terms. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals reversed that conviction in 1978 (Henley v. State, 576 S.W.2d 66), and he was retried in Corpus Christi in June 1979, where a jury again convicted him of six murders on June 27, 1979. The Associated Press reported in 2020 that he was serving six life sentences. Brooks was tried in February 1975 for the June 1973 murder of William Ray Lawrence, 15, was convicted on March 4, 1975, and was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Identification of the victims continued for decades. Forensic work led by Harris County medical examiner's office anthropologist Sharon Derrick identified Randell Lee Harvey in October 2008, Michael Baulch in 2010, Steven Sickman and Roy Bunton in 2011 and Donald Falcon in 2014. ABC13 reported in May 2025 that Derrick's research points to at least 30 victims and that at least one set of remains is still unidentified. The Associated Press reported that Brooks died on May 28, 2020, aged 65, at Hospital Galveston after contracting COVID-19 while held at the Polunsky Unit. The house at 2020 Lamar Drive where Corll was killed was demolished on February 24, 2023, according to ABC13. KPRC reported that the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles denied Henley parole on November 7, 2025, his 25th review, and set his next review roughly ten years away.

Corll was born on December 24, 1939, in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and his family later moved to Houston. He worked in his family's candy businesses in the Houston Heights, including the Corll Candy Company, which closed in June 1968; the free candy he handed out to local children earned him the nicknames 'Candy Man' and 'Pied Piper'. Drafted in August 1964, he served stateside and received an honorable discharge in June 1965. He then worked as an electrician and later a supervisor at Houston Lighting and Power, and in the spring of 1973 he moved into his father's former house on Lamar Drive in Pasadena, where he died.

victimProfile: Young women aged 15 to 23, mostly hitchhiking college students, plus his mother (52) and her friend (59)

summary: Imprisoned. Edmund Kemper was convicted by a Santa Cruz County jury in 1973 of eight counts of first-degree murder for killing six young women, his mother and her friend in 1972 and 1973. He killed his grandparents in 1964 at age 15. Held at Vacaville.
narrative: Edmund Emil Kemper III is a California serial killer convicted by a Santa Cruz County jury in November 1973 of eight counts of first-degree murder. Between May 1972 and April 1973, while living with his mother in Aptos, he killed six young women, most of them hitchhiking college students, then his mother and her closest friend. According to Lookout Santa Cruz and the Wikipedia article, the jury rejected his insanity plea and found him guilty on all eight counts; he received eight concurrent life sentences and has been held since at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville. He had earlier killed his paternal grandparents in 1964, at age 15, a case handled through the juvenile and state hospital system rather than by criminal conviction.

The adult killings began on May 7, 1972, when Kemper picked up two 18-year-old Fresno State students, Mary Ann Pesce and Anita Luchessa, hitchhiking in Berkeley, and killed them, according to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com. On September 14, 1972, he killed 15-year-old Aiko Koo after picking her up on her way to a dance class. On January 7, 1973, he shot 18-year-old Cabrillo College student Cynthia Schall. On February 5, 1973, he picked up Rosalind Thorpe, 23, and Alice Liu, 20, on the University of California, Santa Cruz campus and shot them. The bodies were dismembered and left in the Santa Cruz mountains and on beaches, UPI reported in 1985, and the unsolved killings earned him the press nickname "the Co-ed Killer."

On the weekend of April 20 to 21, 1973, Kemper killed his mother, Clarnell Strandberg, 52, at their home with a hammer and a knife, according to UPI, then invited her friend Sara "Sally" Hallett, 59, to the house and strangled her. He drove east and, from Pueblo, Colorado, telephoned Santa Cruz police to confess. According to the Wikipedia article, officers did not at first take the call seriously; he called again, spoke to an officer he knew, and waited at the phone booth to be arrested. Investigators seized his car on April 27, 1973, according to a photo caption published by KRON4, and his statements led police to evidence.

Kemper was indicted on eight counts of first-degree murder on May 7, 1973, and pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Trial began on October 23, 1973, and he testified on November 1. Three court-appointed psychiatrists found him sane, Newsweek and UPI reported. On November 8, 1973, after about five hours of deliberation, the jury found him sane and guilty on all eight counts. He asked for the death penalty, but California then had a moratorium on capital punishment, so the court imposed concurrent terms of seven years to life on each count, according to the Wikipedia article.

Kemper first became eligible for parole in 1979. According to UPI and Newsweek, the Board of Parole Hearings denied release in 1979, 1980, 1981 and 1982, and again in 1988, 1991, 1994, 2007 and 2017; he waived hearings in 1985, 1997, 2002 and 2012. In July 2024 a three-member panel denied parole for seven more years at a hearing Kemper declined to attend. Lookout Santa Cruz reported that District Attorney Jeff Rosell told the panel Kemper "is still dangerous" and untreated, and that an April 2024 psychiatric evaluation rated him a high risk to reoffend; the board also cited a 2022 incident in which he groped a prison staff member. Kemper, then 75, used a wheelchair and had diabetes, heart disease and a prior stroke. He is next eligible in 2031.

Prison officials described his record as spotless, UPI reported in 1985. Newsweek reported that he scheduled appointments for other inmates, made ceramics and narrated audiobooks for the visually impaired until retiring from those roles after a stroke in 2015.

Kemper was born on December 18, 1948, in Burbank, California. On August 27, 1964, at 15, he shot and killed his grandmother, Maude Kemper, and grandfather, Edmund Kemper Sr., at their ranch near North Fork, according to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com. Court psychiatrists diagnosed paranoid schizophrenia and he was committed to Atascadero State Hospital. He was released to his mother's care on December 18, 1969, his 21st birthday, and moved to Santa Cruz County.

victimProfile: Two women murdered (Sandra Lindsay, 24, and Deborah Dudley, 23) among six Black women aged 18 to 25 abducted in North Philadelphia and held captive in his basement; four survived

summary: Executed in 1999. Gary Heidnik held six women captive in his Philadelphia basement from November 1986 to March 1987; two died. A jury convicted him of two first-degree murders in 1988.
narrative: Gary Michael Heidnik was a Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, man who from November 1986 to March 1987 abducted six women and held them chained in the basement of his house on North Marshall Street, where two of them died. A Philadelphia jury convicted him on July 1, 1988, of two counts of first-degree murder plus kidnapping, rape, aggravated assault and involuntary deviate sexual intercourse counts, and he was sentenced to death. According to the federal opinion in White v. Horn (E.D. Pa. 1999), the Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed the death sentences in Commonwealth v. Heidnik, 526 Pa. 458 (1991). Heidnik was executed by lethal injection on July 6, 1999, and remains the last person put to death by Pennsylvania.

The captives, all Black women, were Josefina Rivera, Sandra Lindsay, Lisa Thomas, Deborah Dudley, Jacqueline Askins and Agnes Adams, as named in CNN reporting carried by CBS News and in a Philadelphia magazine oral history. Rivera, taken first, said Heidnik picked her up on November 25, 1986. Lindsay, who her sister told CNN was intellectually disabled, disappeared the day after Thanksgiving 1986. Thomas was taken shortly before Christmas, Dudley around New Year's Day 1987 and Askins in January 1987. Survivors said the women were chained, kept in a pit dug in the basement floor, starved, beaten and raped.

Lindsay died in February 1987 after being left suspended by her wrists; the prosecutor and defense lawyer both described her death to Philadelphia magazine as suffocation. Heidnik dismembered her body; remains were later found in the house. Dudley died in March 1987 when Heidnik ran an electric current to her chains while she lay in the water-filled pit, according to the Daily Pennsylvanian's account of the Supreme Court record; her body was left in a New Jersey state forest.

The case came to light on March 24, 1987. Heidnik took Rivera out that night to help him pick up Agnes Adams, then let her leave briefly; she called police and said she had been held for four months and that other women remained in the basement. Officers stopped Heidnik's car near 6th and Girard, Rivera identified him, and police entering the house found two women chained in the basement, a third in the pit and human remains in the kitchen. Heidnik was arrested that night.

At trial before Judge Lynne Abraham, defense lawyer A. Charles Peruto Jr. argued insanity; prosecutor Charles Gallagher countered with evidence that Heidnik had grown a $1,500 brokerage deposit into a portfolio worth more than $500,000. The jury rejected the defense and on July 1, 1988, convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder, six of kidnapping, five of rape, four of aggravated assault and two of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, as summarized by Wikipedia and the Daily Pennsylvanian. UPI reported two death sentences plus a cumulative 150 to 300 years; White v. Horn gives the sentencing date as March 2, 1989.

Heidnik never challenged his sentence and asked the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to skip its mandatory review, which the court said the law did not permit. In March 1991 the court, in an opinion by Justice Rolf Larsen, found the evidence sufficient and the death sentences not disproportionate. In April 1997 he came within hours of execution before an anti-death-penalty group and his daughter, Maxine Davidson White, won stays over his competency. A state judge found him competent, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld that finding on August 19, 1998, and in June 1999 it held that White lacked next-friend standing. On July 3, 1999, the federal district court denied her petition for a stay. He was executed at the State Correctional Institution at Rockview in Bellefonte on July 6, 1999.

Heidnik was born on November 22, 1943, in Eastlake, Ohio. According to Wikipedia, he enlisted in the Army at 17, trained as a medic, and was discharged in 1962 after a diagnosis of schizoid personality disorder. In 1971 he incorporated a church and later posed as a bishop, holding services at his home for a congregation largely of people with intellectual disabilities. In 1978 he was convicted of kidnapping and rape after taking a woman from a state hospital on day leave; he was released in April 1983.

summary: Imprisoned. Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer, pleaded guilty in 2003 to 48 murders of women and girls in King County, Washington, between 1982 and 1998, and to a 49th in 2011. He is serving 49 consecutive life sentences without parole.
narrative: Gary Leon Ridgway, known as the Green River Killer, is an American serial killer who murdered women and teenage girls in King County, Washington, between 1982 and 1998. He pleaded guilty in King County Superior Court on November 5, 2003, to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, and on February 18, 2011, to a 49th. He is serving 49 consecutive life sentences without parole at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla. In taped interviews he claimed as many as 71 victims, and investigators continue to examine other cases as possibly connected.

The killings began in the summer of 1982. According to the victim list published by The Seattle Times when Ridgway entered his pleas, the first, Wendy Lee Coffield, 16, disappeared on July 8, 1982; her body was found in the Green River near Kent on July 15. Most of the 48 women and girls he admitted killing disappeared in 1982 and 1983 from the Pacific Highway South corridor between Seattle and Tacoma, where many were working as prostitutes or living as runaways. Ridgway strangled his victims, by hand or with a ligature, and left their bodies in wooded areas south and east of Seattle. Later admitted killings were sporadic: Patricia Barczak in 1986, Roberta Hayes in 1987, Marta Reeves in 1990 and Patricia Yellow Robe in 1998.

The King County Sheriff's Office formed the Green River Task Force in 1982, and Ridgway came to its attention early. The Associated Press reported that in 1983 the boyfriend of victim Marie Malvar told police he had seen her get into Ridgway's pickup; Ridgway denied knowing her and was cleared. In 1984 he contacted the task force himself, passed a polygraph examination and was cleared again. Police collected hair and saliva samples from him in April 1987, but DNA technology of the time could not produce a match.

The break came nearly two decades later. According to The Associated Press, advances in DNA analysis allowed the 1987 saliva sample to be matched to DNA recovered from the bodies of three of the earliest victims. Ridgway, then 52, was arrested on November 30, 2001, as he left his longtime job as a painter at the Kenworth truck plant in Renton.

Facing the death penalty, Ridgway signed a plea agreement with King County prosecutors on June 13, 2003. In exchange for his life, he agreed to confess, to help investigators find victims whose remains had never been located and to plead guilty to any future King County charge corroborated by reliable evidence. He led investigators to the remains of Pammy Avent, Marie Malvar and April Buttram. On November 5, 2003, he pleaded guilty to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, four of them for victims known only as Jane Doe. On December 18, 2003, Judge Richard A. Jones sentenced him to 48 consecutive life terms without parole; The Seattle Times reported a $480,000 fine, $10,000 per victim, and 48 seconds of courtroom silence.

The agreement was invoked again in 2011. On December 21, 2010, teenagers found a skull in a ravine near Auburn that was identified as Rebecca Marrero, 20, last seen leaving a motel in 1982. Ridgway had confessed to killing her in 2003 but was not charged for lack of conclusive evidence. On February 18, 2011, he pleaded guilty to her murder in Kent, and Judge Mary E. Roberts imposed a 49th consecutive life sentence. In September 2024 Ridgway was briefly booked into the King County jail on an investigative hold; KOMO News reported the sheriff's office was still examining potentially related cases. In December 2025 the Department of Corrections denied reports that he was receiving end-of-life care.

Ridgway was born in Salt Lake City, Utah, on February 18, 1949, grew up in the SeaTac area and graduated from Tyee High School in 1969. He served in the U.S. Navy, including a deployment to Vietnam, was married three times, and worked for about three decades as a spray painter at the Kenworth plant before his arrest.

name: Israel Keyes
victimProfile: Strangers chosen at random, including a teenage barista in Anchorage and a married couple in their fifties in Vermont
captureMethod: Stopped by Texas Highway Patrol near Lufkin while driving a rental car matching a bulletin, after ransom money deposited into Samantha Koenig's account was tracked to ATM withdrawals in Alaska, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas.
fateDetail: Found dead in his cell at the Anchorage Correctional Complex on the morning of December 2, 2012, while awaiting a March 2013 federal trial
summary: Died before trial. Israel Keyes was indicted for the 2012 kidnapping and killing of Samantha Koenig in Anchorage, confessed to murdering Bill and Lorraine Currier in Vermont and five others, and died by suicide in custody in December 2012.
narrative: Israel Keyes was an Anchorage contractor and Army veteran indicted in federal court in April 2012 for the kidnapping and killing of 18-year-old Samantha Koenig. In custody he confessed to killing William and Lorraine Currier of Essex, Vermont, in June 2011. He was never convicted: he died by suicide in the Anchorage Correctional Complex in December 2012, about three months before trial. According to U.S. Attorney Karen Loeffler, quoted by the Anchorage Daily News, Keyes said he had killed Koenig, the Curriers and five others. In August 2013 the FBI said it had linked 11 killings to him based on his statements, most unnamed and unverified.

The Vermont State Police record that Bill Currier, 50, and Lorraine Currier, 55, were last seen at their Essex home on the evening of June 8, 2011, and that evidence at the house suggested they had not left voluntarily. According to the Anchorage Daily News, Keyes later said he had flown to Chicago, driven to Vermont, taken the couple in their own car to an abandoned farmhouse, shot Bill Currier and strangled Lorraine Currier. The farmhouse had been demolished before investigators arrived, and the bodies have not been located. Keyes was never charged in Vermont.

Samantha Koenig was abducted from the Common Grounds coffee stand in Anchorage on February 1, 2012. According to the account released by Anchorage police and the FBI in December 2012, reported by Alaska Public Media, Keyes approached in a ski mask near closing, bound her with zip ties and drove her to a shed at his home, where he sexually assaulted and strangled her. The next day he left on a pre-planned cruise from New Orleans. After returning on February 17 he photographed the body with a dated newspaper and left a typed $30,000 ransom demand in a city park. The remains were placed under the ice of Matanuska Lake; FBI divers recovered them in early April.

The ransom led to his arrest. The U.S. Attorney's Office stated that Koenig's family deposited reward money into the account linked to her stolen debit card so withdrawals could be tracked, and that Keyes withdrew money from ATMs in Alaska, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas. On March 13, 2012, a Texas Highway Patrol corporal stopped a white Ford Focus matching a bulletin near Lufkin, Texas; officers found Koenig's phone and ATM card. Returned to Alaska on a federal access-device fraud charge, the Anchorage Daily News reported, he soon confessed and told investigators where to find her body.

On April 18, 2012, the U.S. Attorney announced a federal grand jury indictment on three counts: kidnapping resulting in death, receiving and possessing ransom money, and access device fraud. The kidnapping count carried a maximum penalty of death or life imprisonment. Keyes pleaded not guilty to all three counts before U.S. District Judge Michael Thompson. In May 2012 he tried to escape by vaulting the courtroom rail and was subdued with a Taser. Trial was set for March 2013.

In FBI interviews Keyes described other killings. According to the Anchorage Daily News, he admitted to four murders in Washington state, where he lived from about 2001 to 2007, and one on the East Coast in 2009, with the body left in New York. He named none of those victims, and none has been identified. The FBI said he buried caches of weapons and body-disposal items, two of which were recovered in Alaska and New York, and that he financed his travel partly through bank robberies.

Keyes was found dead in his cell on the morning of December 2, 2012; Alaska State Troopers called it an apparent suicide, and Wikipedia gives the date of death as December 1. Because he died before trial, no court ever ruled on the Koenig charges or any other killing. In August 2013 the FBI released a timeline of his travels and said three further killings had been added based on his statements.

Keyes was born on January 7, 1978, in Richmond, Utah, according to Wikipedia. He served in the U.S. Army from 1998 to 2001, lived in Neah Bay, Washington, and moved to Anchorage in March 2007, where he ran a construction business and lived with his partner and daughter.

name: Jerry Brudos
victimProfile: Young women aged 19 to 23, abducted from parking areas, a shopping center, a roadside and a door-to-door sales call in the Salem and Portland areas
captureMethod: Identified after an Oregon State University student he had phoned reported his call to police, then confirmed through a search warrant on his home and his confession
sentence: Three consecutive life terms with the possibility of parole, on guilty pleas to three counts of first-degree murder (Marion County Circuit Court, June 27, 1969); affirmed on appeal in 1970
fateDetail: Oregon State Penitentiary, Salem; died of liver cancer after nearly 37 years in custody
summary: Convicted on guilty pleas to three first-degree murders in Oregon in 1969 and sentenced to three consecutive life terms. Jerry Brudos confessed to four killings of young women in 1968 and 1969 and died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in 2006.
narrative: Jerome Henry Brudos, known as Jerry Brudos, pleaded guilty in June 1969 to three counts of first-degree murder for the killings of young women in the Salem and Portland areas of Oregon in 1968 and 1969. According to the Oregon Court of Appeals in State v. Brudos (1970), he entered the pleas orally and in writing with the advice of counsel and received three consecutive life sentences. Police attributed four murders to him and he admitted all four, but he was never tried for the fourth because the victim's body was not recovered. He died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in 2006.

According to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com, the first victim was Linda Slawson, a 19-year-old encyclopedia saleswoman from Aloha, who called at Brudos's home in the Portland area on January 26, 1968, and was killed there; her body was never found. On November 26, 1968, Jan Whitney, 23, disappeared after her car broke down on Interstate 5 between Salem and Albany. Brudos later admitted stopping for her and strangling her in his car. Her remains were recovered from the Willamette River near Independence after his conviction and identified by dental records.

Karen Sprinker, an 18-year-old Oregon State University student, was abducted at gunpoint from a department store parking garage in downtown Salem on March 27, 1969. Linda Salee, 22, of Beaverton, was taken from the Lloyd Center shopping area in Portland on April 23, 1969. In May 1969 both bodies were found in the Long Tom River, weighted with automobile parts and bound with cord. In the same week as the Salee abduction, two other young women escaped attempted abductions in Portland; one later identified Brudos.

Investigators noticed that the knots on both river victims matched and, because Sprinker was an OSU student, interviewed women on the Corvallis campus. One student reported that a caller had asked her for a date, and police asked her to report any further contact. When Brudos called again, officers were present at the meeting. According to the Wikipedia article, his home was searched under warrant on May 26, 1969, yielding nylon rope and photographs of the victims, and Oregon state troopers took him into custody on May 29 after finding him hiding in the family station wagon. In early June he confessed to the four murders and to earlier assaults.

Brudos was arraigned on June 4, 1969, in Marion County and initially pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Court-appointed psychiatrists found him legally sane. On June 27, 1969, before Circuit Judge Val D. Sloper, he pleaded guilty to the first-degree murders of Sprinker, Whitney and Salee and was sentenced to three consecutive life terms with the possibility of parole. His wife, Ralphene Brudos, was indicted in August 1969 in connection with the Sprinker murder and was acquitted at trial.

The Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions and sentences on July 9, 1970, holding that consecutive life terms were permissible and that any challenge to the pleas had to be raised through post-conviction relief; the Oregon Supreme Court denied review that September. Brudos then sought post-conviction relief, arguing his pleas were not knowing and voluntary. According to Brudos v. Cupp (1977), the post-conviction court rejected that claim and the Court of Appeals upheld the denial of his request to move the hearing out of Marion County. The Wikipedia article reports that later appeals failed and parole was repeatedly denied over the objections of the victims' families.

Brudos spent nearly 37 years at the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem, where he held clerical jobs. He died there of liver cancer on March 28, 2006, at age 67, described by state officials as the longest-held inmate in the Oregon prison system.

Brudos was born on January 31, 1939, in Webster, South Dakota, and grew up in Oregon. According to the Wikipedia article, he was arrested in 1956 at age 17 for assaulting a girl and spent nine months under psychiatric evaluation at the Oregon State Hospital, graduated from Corvallis High School in 1957, was discharged from the Army in 1959 and married in 1961. He was living in Salem with his wife and two children at the time of the 1969 murders.

name: Joel Rifkin
victimProfile: Women aged roughly 21 to 41, most of them sex workers picked up in Manhattan
captureMethod: Stopped by state troopers for a missing rear license plate, fled, crashed, and was found with a victim's body in his pickup truck
sentence: Aggregate 203 years to life: 25 years to life by jury verdict in Nassau County (1994) plus consecutive terms on guilty pleas in Suffolk, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties (1995 to 1996)
fateDetail: Clinton Correctional Facility, Dannemora, New York
summary: Imprisoned. Joel Rifkin, a Long Island landscaper, confessed to killing 17 women in New York between 1989 and 1993 and was convicted of nine murders after a 1993 traffic stop revealed a body in his truck.
narrative: Joel David Rifkin is a convicted serial killer who murdered women in New York City and on Long Island between 1989 and 1993. According to the New York State Police, he admitted to 16 murders beyond the one for which he was arrested, 17 in all. He was convicted of nine murders in jury and plea proceedings in Nassau, Suffolk, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties between 1994 and 1996 and, according to NBC News, is serving an aggregate sentence of 203 years. He is held at Clinton Correctional Facility.

The known victims were women, most of them sex workers picked up in Manhattan, who were strangled after sexual encounters and whose bodies were left in waterways, wooded areas and other sites around the region. According to the Wikipedia article, the first killing was that of Heidi Balch, 25, in early 1989; a head found at a Hopewell Township, New Jersey golf course in March 1989 was identified as hers only in 2013. Other bodies were recovered from New York City rivers and creeks, upstate New York and Long Island between 1991 and 1993. Two victims were never found, and a woman found in a drum in Newtown Creek in May 1992 has never been identified.

The series ended with a traffic stop. According to the New York State Police, at about 3:15 a.m. on June 28, 1993, troopers Deborah Spaargaren and Sean Ruane tried to pull over a 1984 Mazda pickup on the Southern State Parkway because it had no rear plate. The driver fled at up to 90 mph, struck a light pole on Old Country Road after a 20 to 25 minute chase and was taken into custody. An inventory search of the truck found the body of Tiffany Bresciani, 22, who had disappeared four days earlier. At the station house Rifkin admitted to 16 further killings; a task force recovered the remains of 15 victims across 10 jurisdictions.

Rifkin was tried first in Nassau County for Bresciani's murder and raised an insanity defense. According to United Press International, on May 9, 1994 a jury deliberated just over two hours before convicting him of second-degree murder and first-degree reckless endangerment arising from the chase. Judge Ira Wexner sentenced him on June 8, 1994; wire reports described the combined term as 27 years to life. In December 2001 the Appellate Division, Second Department, held that statements Rifkin made at the crash scene after being handcuffed should have been suppressed because they preceded Miranda warnings, but affirmed the conviction in light of the otherwise overwhelming evidence, finding the later station-house confession voluntary.

The other convictions came by plea. In Suffolk County he admitted murdering Leah Evens and Lauren Marquez, both 28, and on September 18, 1995 Judge John Jones imposed two consecutive terms of 25 years to life, according to wire reports in The Spokesman-Review. In Brooklyn he pleaded guilty on December 1, 1995 to three counts of second-degree murder for Lorraine Orvieto, Mary Ann Holloman and an unidentified woman; UPI reported that on December 12 he received life with a 75-year minimum, consecutive to his earlier terms. According to Wikipedia, a further life sentence followed in January 1996 in the Bronx for the murder of Jenny Soto.

On January 25, 1996, Queens Supreme Court Justice Robert Hanophy added 25 years for the murder of Iris Sanchez, 25, whose body had been found under mattresses near Kennedy Airport. UPI reported that Rifkin, who by then had accumulated 177 years for seven murders, apologized to the victims' families and called himself a monster; the judge noted he was not eligible for New York's newly restored death penalty. In March 2013 Hopewell Township police announced that the 1989 remains had been identified through DNA from the victim's mother as Heidi Balch; NBC News reported that Rifkin would not be charged in New Jersey.

Rifkin was born in New York City on January 20, 1959, and was adopted as an infant by Bernard and Jeanne Rifkin of East Meadow, Long Island, according to Wikipedia. He graduated from East Meadow High School in 1977, attended several colleges without earning a degree and worked as a self-employed landscaper. He was 34 when arrested.

name: Joseph James DeAngelo

victims.suspected: 13 murders; prosecutors also attribute about 50 rapes and more than 120 burglaries

victimProfile: Men and women attacked in their homes at night, often couples; earlier victims were women and girls raped during home invasions
captureMethod: Forensic genetic genealogy on the GEDmatch database pointed investigators to his family, and crime-scene DNA was then matched to samples taken from his car door handle and a discarded tissue.

summary: Imprisoned for life. Joseph DeAngelo, the Golden State Killer, pleaded guilty in 2020 to 13 California murders committed from 1975 to 1986 and admitted dozens of rapes; he was identified in 2018 through forensic genetic genealogy.
narrative: Joseph James DeAngelo is the former California police officer identified in 2018 as the Golden State Killer, the offender earlier known as the Visalia Ransacker, the East Area Rapist and the Original Night Stalker. On June 29, 2020, he pleaded guilty in Sacramento County Superior Court to 13 counts of first-degree murder with special circumstances and 13 counts of kidnapping, and under the plea he admitted dozens of uncharged rapes. NBC News reported that prosecutors described crimes against 87 victims at 53 crime scenes in 11 California counties between 1975 and 1986. On August 21, 2020, Judge Michael Bowman sentenced him to consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole.

The first killing DeAngelo admitted was the September 11, 1975 shooting of Claude Snelling in Visalia, Tulare County, during the period when the Visalia Ransacker was burglarizing homes there. According to the Wikipedia article, the East Area Rapist home-invasion attacks began in Rancho Cordova, near Sacramento, on June 18, 1976, and continued into 1979; Brian and Katie Maggiore were shot to death in Rancho Cordova on February 2, 1978. The attacks then moved to Southern California. According to the Wikipedia article and charges reported by NBC News, Robert Offerman and Debra Manning were killed in Goleta on December 30, 1979; Lyman and Charlene Smith in Ventura on March 13, 1980; Keith and Patrice Harrington in Dana Point on August 19, 1980; Manuela Witthuhn in Irvine on February 6, 1981; Cheri Domingo and Gregory Sanchez in Goleta on July 27, 1981; and Janelle Cruz in Irvine in May 1986. The later victims were bludgeoned in their homes after being bound.

DNA testing eventually linked the Southern California murders to the East Area Rapist attacks. In 2018 investigators uploaded a DNA profile from crime-scene evidence to the public genealogy database GEDmatch, built family trees from distant relatives who matched, and narrowed the candidates to DeAngelo. NBC News reported that Sacramento County Sheriff Scott Jones said investigators confirmed the match with discarded DNA after six days of surveillance; according to the Wikipedia article the samples came from his car door handle and a tissue in his trash. He was arrested at his Citrus Heights home on April 24, 2018, at age 72, in the first widely publicized arrest made through forensic genetic genealogy.

NBC News reported that at an August 2018 arraignment DeAngelo faced 13 murder counts across Sacramento, Santa Barbara, Tulare, Ventura and Orange counties and 13 kidnapping counts in Sacramento and Contra Costa counties; the kidnapping charges were used because California's statute of limitations barred prosecution of the rapes themselves. The district attorneys agreed to consolidate all of the cases in Sacramento.

The 2020 plea agreement spared DeAngelo the death penalty. The Associated Press, in a report carried by PBS NewsHour, said prosecutors had initially sought death but accepted life terms, citing California's execution moratorium, the pandemic and the ages of the defendant, victims and witnesses. Sentencing followed three days of victim impact statements in a university ballroom. DeAngelo, then 74, rose from a wheelchair and told the court he was sorry to everyone he had hurt, ABC News reported. The AP reported that Judge Bowman imposed 11 consecutive life terms without parole on the murder counts, additional life terms on the remaining counts and eight years for enhancements. He waived his right to appeal.

According to the Wikipedia article, DeAngelo is held in protective custody at California State Prison, Corcoran, and DNA testing has excluded him from several other unsolved killings once speculatively linked to the case.

DeAngelo was born on November 8, 1945, in Bath, New York, according to the Wikipedia article. He served in the Navy during the Vietnam War, studied police science and criminal justice, and worked as a police officer in Exeter from 1973 to 1976 and in Auburn from 1976 to 1979. NBC News reported that he was fired from the Auburn department in 1979 after being arrested for shoplifting a hammer and dog repellent. He raised three daughters in Citrus Heights and later worked as a truck mechanic. His wife filed for divorce after his arrest.

name: Nannie Doss
victimProfile: Members of her own family: four husbands, two daughters, her mother, a sister, a mother-in-law and two grandchildren
captureMethod: After her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, died in Tulsa in October 1954, his physician pressed for an autopsy, which found a large quantity of arsenic; she was arrested and confessed under questioning.

summary: Died in prison. Nannie Doss pleaded guilty in 1955 to poisoning her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, in Tulsa, Oklahoma, confessed to killing four husbands, and is linked to as many as 11 family deaths from 1927 to 1954. She died at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in 1965.
narrative: Nannie Doss, born Nancy Agnes Hazel, was a serial poisoner whose victims were members of her own family in Alabama, North Carolina, Kansas and Oklahoma between 1927 and 1954. She was convicted of one murder: on May 17, 1955, she pleaded guilty in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to killing her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, and was sentenced to life imprisonment. According to the Encyclopedia of Alabama, she confessed under interrogation to killing four husbands. The Wikipedia article and an Oklahoma Gazette retrospective attribute as many as 11 deaths to her, among them two of her daughters, her mother, a sister, a mother-in-law and two grandchildren. She was never charged in any death other than that of Samuel Doss.

The Encyclopedia of Alabama records that she married Charles Braggs in 1921, at about 16, after the two met at the Linen Thread Company in Anniston, Alabama. Two of their four daughters died in 1927, with the deaths attributed at the time to food poisoning. The couple divorced in 1928, and Braggs was the only one of her five husbands to survive the marriage. In 1929 she married Frank Harrelson, whom she met through a lonely hearts column. Harrelson died on September 15, 1945; by her later account, she had put rat poison in his whiskey. A grandson, Robert, died of asphyxia at age two while in her care, and she collected a $500 life insurance policy.

Her third husband, Arlie Lanning of Lexington, North Carolina, died of what was recorded as heart failure, with no autopsy performed; the Encyclopedia of Alabama dates his death to 1950, while the Oklahoma Gazette gives 1952. The Wikipedia article states that Lanning's mother died in her sleep while Doss lived in the household, and that her sister Dovie died soon after Doss came to stay with her. In October 1952 she married Richard L. Morton of Emporia, Kansas. Her mother, Louisa Hazle, came to live with the couple and died within days, in January 1953. Morton died on May 19, 1953, after, the Encyclopedia of Alabama reports, drinking coffee laced with arsenic.

In June 1953 she married Samuel Doss, a Nazarene minister, in Tulsa, Oklahoma. In the autumn of 1954 he was hospitalised with a severe digestive illness, was sent home on October 5 and died about a week later, on October 12 according to the Wikipedia article. His physician insisted on an autopsy, which found a large quantity of arsenic. Doss was arrested in Tulsa in October 1954 and, during questioning, confessed to killing four husbands; the Encyclopedia of Alabama reports she did so in exchange for being allowed to keep a romance magazine. Her habit of laughing while recounting the deaths produced the nickname the Giggling Granny. The same source states that exhumations reportedly confirmed rat poison or arsenic in several of the bodies.

Oklahoma prosecuted her for a single count of murder, that of Samuel Doss. The prosecutor, according to the Wikipedia article, was J. Howard Edmondson, later governor of Oklahoma. She pleaded guilty on May 17, 1955, and received a life sentence; the Wikipedia article and a syndicated history column published by the Albuquerque Journal both report that the state did not seek the death penalty because she was a woman. The Encyclopedia of Alabama notes that North Carolina, Kansas and Alabama also brought charges, but she was never tried outside Oklahoma.

She served her sentence at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester, where she died of leukemia in the prison hospital ward on June 2, 1965, at age 59. She was buried at Oak Hill Memorial Park in McAlester. The Oklahoma Gazette has written that her case figures in the history of Oklahoma's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, as an example of suspicious deaths that went uninvestigated before the state had a medical examiner system.

She was born on November 4, 1905, in Blue Mountain, Calhoun County, Alabama, one of five children of Jim and Louisa Hazle. The Encyclopedia of Alabama describes her father as abusive and says he kept the children out of school to work the family farm. At about age seven she suffered a head injury in a train incident, which she later blamed for headaches and blackouts.

summary: On death row in California since 1989. Randy Kraft was convicted by an Orange County jury of murdering 16 young men between 1972 and 1983; a coded list found at his 1983 arrest is believed to reference up to 67 victims in California, Oregon and Michigan.
narrative: Randy Steven Kraft is a California serial killer convicted of murdering 16 young men in Southern California between 1972 and 1983. According to the California Supreme Court's 2000 opinion in People v. Kraft, an Orange County jury convicted him in May 1989 of 16 counts of first-degree murder, one count of sodomy and one count of mayhem, and he was sentenced to death on November 29, 1989. Investigators attribute more deaths to him: the Orange County Sheriff's Department said in 2025 that it believes he is responsible for more than 60 killings in California, six in Oregon and two in Michigan. He has never confessed and, the Associated Press reported in 2025, denies killing anyone.

The court opinion sets out the 16 murders. The earliest victim, Marine Edward Daniel Moore, was found strangled near a Long Beach-area freeway off-ramp on December 26, 1972. Others followed through the 1970s, including Ronald Wiebe, Keith Crotwell, Mark Hall, Scott Hughes, Roland Young, Richard Keith, Keith Klingbeil, Michael Inderbieten, Donald Crisel and Robert Loggins, with a final cluster in 1983 of Eric Church, Geoffrey Nelson and Rodger DeVaul. Most were strangled with a ligature or suffocated after being given alcohol and sedatives, and their bodies were left beside freeways in Orange and Los Angeles counties. The opinion notes that physical evidence, including a thumbprint at the Hall scene and victims' property and photographs found in his home and car, linked Kraft to eight murders; the rest rested on the common method and his written list.

Kraft was arrested early on May 14, 1983. According to the opinion, California Highway Patrol officers saw his car weaving on Interstate 5 in southern Orange County and arrested him for drunk driving; his passenger, 25-year-old Marine Terry Gambrel, was dead of ligature strangulation, with a vial of Kraft's prescription sedative on the floor. A notebook in the car held a sheet of 61 cryptic handwritten entries. Prosecutors linked 13 to the charged murders, eight to Oregon and Michigan killings and 21 to uncharged victims, hence the press name Scorecard Killer.

The trial opened in Orange County Superior Court in September 1988 and ran about 13 months, according to reporting summarized in the Wikipedia article. The jury returned guilty verdicts on May 12, 1989 and a death verdict on August 11, 1989. Death was imposed on the 11 murders committed after 1978; the five earlier murders drew consecutive 25-years-to-life terms, stayed. The CDCR condemned list records the sentence date as November 29, 1989.

In the penalty phase, the opinion records, prosecutors presented eight uncharged murders in Oregon and Michigan. Oregon victims found near Interstate 5 between July 1980 and December 1982 included Michael O'Fallon, Michael Cluck, Brian Whitcher, Anthony Silveira and an unidentified man; travel records placed Kraft in the Portland area on each date, and several victims' belongings were in his home. In Michigan, Dennis Alt and Christopher Schoenborn were found strangled in Kent County on December 9, 1982, last seen at the Grand Rapids hotel where Kraft was staying.

On August 10, 2000, the California Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the judgment in its entirety in an opinion by Justice Werdegar. Kraft remains under sentence of death; California executions have been halted by a gubernatorial moratorium since 2019, and official and AP reporting in 2023 and 2025 placed him at San Quentin.

DNA work has continued to develop the case. In November 2023 the Orange County Sheriff's Department used genetic genealogy to identify a John Doe found in Laguna Hills in 1974 as Michael Ray Schlicht, 17, of Cedar Rapids, Iowa, calling him a presumed early Kraft victim. In May 2025 the department and Oregon State Police identified the 1980 Oregon John Doe as Larry Eugene Parks, a 30-year-old Vietnam veteran, and Oregon State Police named Kraft the sole person of interest.

Kraft was born in Long Beach, California, on March 19, 1945, according to the Wikipedia article, graduated from Claremont Men's College in 1968 and received a general discharge from the U.S. Air Force in 1969. He worked as a computer programmer; the court opinion notes his employment with Lear Siegler from 1980 to 1983, whose business travel coincided with the Oregon and Michigan murders.
